title: Pork Slaughtering Procedures in the Clean Area

lessons.title: Entering the clean area and opening the carcass
lessons.html:
The clean area

The clean area begins after the pig carcass has been scalded, de-haired, singed, scraped, shaved and washed. From here on the meat inside the carcass will be opened up, so hygiene is even more important. Germs from the gut, from hands or from dirty knives can spoil meat and make people sick.

Before you start work

  • Wear clean protective clothing in the colour for the clean area: overall or coat, apron, hairnet, and white boots.
  • Wash your hands and arms with soap and warm water. Wash boots at the boot wash.
  • Check that your knives are sharp and sterilised. Use the knife sterilizer between carcasses and whenever a knife gets dirty.
  • Wear your cut-resistant glove and chain-mail apron if your plant gives them.

Opening the carcass

  1. Bunging (freeing the rectum). The anus is cut loose with a knife or bung tool and tied or bagged so that dung cannot leak out onto the meat.
  2. Opening the belly. The belly is cut open from the top (between the hind legs) down to the breastbone. Hold the knife with the blade pointing outwards and use your other hand or the knife handle to protect the guts. A cut into the stomach or intestines spills dung onto the carcass.
  3. Opening the chest. The breastbone is split with a knife or saw so the pluck (heart, lungs, liver) can come out.

If you cut a gut by mistake, stop. Tell your supervisor. The dirty part must be trimmed off under the supervision of the meat inspector. Never wipe dung off with a cloth or wash it in and carry on.

lessons.title: Evisceration, head and splitting
lessons.html:
Evisceration

Evisceration means taking out the guts and organs. It has two parts:

  • Rough offal (white offal): stomach and intestines. These are lifted out in one piece and put into the correct tray or chute. Keep them away from the carcass.
  • Red offal (pluck): heart, lungs, liver, and often the tongue and throat. These are hung or placed so that they stay matched to their own carcass for the meat inspector.

Matching is very important. The meat inspector looks at the organs and the carcass together. If disease is found in the organs, the inspector must know exactly which carcass it came from. Use the tag, number or tray system of your abattoir.

Head

In many pork abattoirs the head stays on the carcass until inspection, or it is removed and kept with the carcass. The meat inspector cuts and checks lymph nodes in the head and neck. Follow your plant procedure.

Splitting

The carcass is split down the middle of the backbone into two sides with a splitting saw or cleaver. A good split is straight, through the centre of the spine. A bad split wastes meat.

Saw safety

  • Only trained, authorised workers may use the splitting saw.
  • Keep both hands on the handles. Never put a hand in front of the blade.
  • Check the guard and the emergency stop before you start.
  • Wear ear and eye protection if your plant requires it.
  • Clean and sterilise the saw between carcasses as the procedure says.

Never remove spinal cord, organs or parts that the inspector still needs to see before inspection is done.

lessons.title: Inspection, trimming, washing and chilling
lessons.html:
Meat inspection

Every pork carcass and its organs must be inspected by a meat inspector before it can be sold. This is part of the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. The inspector looks, feels and cuts at set places. The inspector may pass the carcass, pass it with trimming, detain it for more checks, or condemn it.

  • Do not move a detained carcass from the detain rail without permission.
  • Condemned meat goes into marked bins and is destroyed as the law and plant procedure require.
  • Never hide or remove a sign of disease.

Trimming

Trimmers remove bruises, small dirty spots, blood clots, and parts the inspector asks to be removed. Trim with a sterile knife. Put trimmings into the correct container. Sterilise the knife after each trim.

Final wash and weighing

The carcass sides are washed with clean, potable water to remove bone dust and small blood spots. Washing does not remove dung; dung must be trimmed off. The carcass is then weighed, marked and classified as your plant procedure says.

Chilling

The sides go into the chiller (cold room). Cooling quickly slows the growth of germs. Hang carcasses so they do not touch each other, the walls or the floor, so that cold air can move around them. Keep chiller doors closed and report a chiller that is not cold. Do not overload the chiller.

Key points

  • Clean clothing, clean hands and sterile knives are essential in the clean area.
  • Bung the rectum and open the belly carefully so guts are not cut.
  • Keep organs matched to their own carcass for the meat inspector.
  • Only trained workers use the splitting saw, with hands away from the blade.
  • Dung is trimmed off, not washed off.
  • Chill carcasses quickly with space around each one.

quiz.question: Why is the rectum (bung) freed and tied or bagged?

options.text: To stop dung leaking onto the meat
So the meat inspector can see it better

quiz.question: Which organs are called red offal (pluck)?
Why must organs stay matched to their own carcass?

options.text: So they can be sold separately
To save space in the chiller
So the meat inspector knows which carcass any disease came from

quiz.question: You accidentally cut an intestine and dung spills on the carcass. What do you do?

options.text: Wipe it off with a cloth and carry on
Wash it off with the hose
Hide it so you do not get into trouble
Stop, tell your supervisor, and have the dirty part trimmed off

quiz.question: Why are carcasses hung with space between them in the chiller?

options.text: So cold air can move around each carcass

quiz.question: Any worker may use the splitting saw if the trained operator is on a break.
A detained carcass must not be moved from the detain rail without permission.
What should you do before starting work in the clean area? (select all that apply)

options.text: Wash hands and arms with soap and warm water
Put on clean protective clothing for the clean area
Bring your knife from the dirty area without cleaning it
Check that your knives are sharp and sterilised
